Only the part of the volume that the truncated fetch returned was read, and the pages or sections seen are unknown. No renewal was found in the portion fetched. Needs a manual page-by-page check before treating the print as verified public domain.

evidence.note: This is a sound film. The recorded soundtrack would normally share the print's status, so it depends on the print's renewal result. I did not confirm the composers or any separate music copyright.
The short stars Superman, a character that comes from DC's comics and is still claimed by DC. The film's own copyright status does not free the character.
Superman and his logo are, to my knowledge, actively held as marks by DC. I did not fetch a registration record to confirm this.

editorial:
The Bulleteers is a 1942 animated Superman short. A creator would want it for its period animation and look.

The rights trap is the character, not the print. Even if the film's own copyright was never renewed, Superman remains DC's property as a character and trademark. Reusing the footage unchanged is a separate question from using Superman in new work. I have not confirmed the renewal check by hand, so treat the print status as open until the 1969 and 1970 renewal volumes are read page by page.
faq: Can I upload The Bulleteers to my own channel?

Not safely yet. A machine scan of only the part of each 1969 and 1970 catalog volume that was fetched found no renewal, and the pages read are unknown. Read the 1969 and 1970 motion-picture volumes by hand to confirm. Superman trademarks may still cause platform takedowns.
Can I make new Superman stories or merchandise from it?
No. The film's status does not free the Superman character or logo. DC still claims the character and the marks.
